issues.legal_issue: Grouping the separate holdings of family members to determine an agricultural land ceiling does not violate the second proviso to Article 31A(1), and the law need not use one uniform ceiling for every individual.
material_facts: The land-ceiling law grouped an individual’s land with separately held land of the individual’s spouse and minor children to determine the family’s ceiling.
The law did not merge or extinguish the family members’ separate ownership or legal personalities, and it allowed holders to select land to retain in proportion to their separate holdings.
The law provided for compensation for land acquired in excess of the ceiling.
The law defined a person to include a joint family, while the General Clauses Act definition included bodies of individuals.
issues.conclusion: The grouping provision was valid. The second proviso to Article 31A(1) neither requires a single uniform ceiling nor prescribes a particular method for imposing different ceilings on differently situated individuals; the statutory grouping did not alter the family members’ separate legal status or ownership.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(1), including its second proviso, does not prohibit different ceiling limits for individuals or classes of individuals differently situated, and does not require those limits to be prescribed directly in a single provision. The term person has no fixed concept that prevents a law from grouping family members’ separate holdings for ceiling computation. Article 367 applies definitions in the General Clauses Act, 1897, including section 3(42), for interpreting the Constitution, but that definition does not bar such grouping. Section 6(2) of the Gujarat Agricultural Land Ceiling Act grouped holdings for determining the ceiling without merging separate legal personalities or ownership. Pritam Singh v. State of Punjab was distinguished; Kunjukutty Sahib v. State of Kerala was relied on regarding the effect of a changed ceiling limit.

predicates.land_ceiling_law_challenge: A person challenges a law that limits how much agricultural land may be held.
predicates.separate_family_holdings_grouped_for_cei: The law counts separately held land of family members together when determining the applicable ceiling.
predicates.separate_ownership_preserved: The law leaves the family members’ separate ownership and legal identities intact.
predicates.holders_can_select_land_to_retain: The law allows the holders to select which land to retain, with the retained land reflecting their separate holdings.

issues.definition: When a land-ceiling challenge concerns family members’ separately held land counted together for the ceiling, grouping is permitted if their separate ownership remains intact or they can select land to retain.

issues.legal_issue: A law included in the Ninth Schedule is protected against a challenge based on alleged violation of Part III rights, including rights under the second proviso to Article 31A(1).
material_facts: The challenged land-ceiling law had been included in the Ninth Schedule.
The challenge alleged that grouping family members’ holdings circumvented the second proviso to Article 31A(1) and exceeded legislative power.

The Court held that the proviso protects and confers rights to compensation, and found no issue of legislative competence of the kind that would arise from legislation trespassing on an exclusive legislative domain.
issues.conclusion: Article 31B protected the challenged provisions from the asserted Part III-based attack. The second proviso to Article 31A(1) confers rights concerning compensation and did not impose the asserted limit on legislative competence.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B provides that laws and provisions specified in the Ninth Schedule are not void on the ground that they are inconsistent with, or take away or abridge, rights conferred by Part III. The protection can apply even where the alleged infringement concerns rights protected by the second proviso to Article 31A(1), because that proviso protects and confers individual rights to compensation. The Court relied on H.H. Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalavaru v. State of Kerala concerning the effect of Article 31B and held that Article 31A and Article 31B may provide dual protection.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A person challenges the validity of a law concerning land reform.
predicates.law_included_in_protected_schedule: The challenged law has been included in the constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from Part III-based invalidity.
predicates.challenge_alleges_part_three_rights_viol: The challenge alleges that the law violates rights protected by Part III of the Constitution.

issues.definition: If a land-reform law is challenged on the ground that it violates Part III rights and it has been included in the protected schedule, the law is protected against that challenge.
